title: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The Smith-Morra — sacrifice the d-pawn for rapid development and open lines against the Sicilian.
Against the solid e6 system, one of Black's better tries, the theoretical move is coming up.

Bc4 — deeply counter-intuitive, since it seems to bite on granite against e6, but the point is hidden: if a knight later lands on d5 and Black takes, the e6-pawn vanishes and the bishop's diagonal blazes open.
moves.teaches: A bishop that looks blunted by a pawn can be aimed at the moment that pawn is forced to disappear.

moves.spoken: Rather than hunt for something insane, just castle — put the decision off and trust straightforward development.
moves.teaches: When no forcing idea works, don't force it; a calm developing move keeps the initiative.

moves.spoken: Now simple chess with an edge: sling the knight into d5. Probably not objectively sound, but it's a very real practical try.

The knight lunges at the bishop, but this sacrifice isn't preposterous — you should feel intuitively why it works. Black is utterly undeveloped, neither bishop is out, castling is far away, and the e-file is wide open for Re1-check and d6 ideas. In the gambit mindset you don't reflexively defend the attacked bishop — you move it by choice, keeping every threat alive.
moves.teaches: A sacrifice is justified when the defender is undeveloped and the lines against his king are already open.
